title: The cloak with fifty-two tassels
hookLine: released from Gwalior fort, tradition says he left only if fifty-two imprisoned princes could come, holding his cloak

cards: You've been locked up a long time, months, maybe years. Then one morning the guard comes with news: the emperor has ordered your release. The gate is right there.
But look around the cells. There are other prisoners here, dozens of them, held for politics, forgotten, with no one coming for them. The order says nothing about them.
Only you. Sikh tradition tells what Guru Hargobind said when that order came to him in the fort at Gwalior. It's a story that ends with lamps.

teach.b: Some time after he built the Akal Takht, Guru Hargobind was imprisoned by the emperor Jahangir in the great fort at Gwalior.

Why, and for how long, the sources don't agree: some point to an unpaid fine left over from his father's case, some to the Guru's growing army, some to court enemies. Historians still argue over the dates.
What Sikhs remember is how it ended.
In the fort, tradition says, were fifty-two princes, rajas from the hill kingdoms, held as political prisoners, and the Guru befriended them.
When the order came to free him, he refused to go alone: let these princes come too.

teach.h: AS MANY AS HOLD YOUR CLOAK.
teach.b: The emperor, tradition says, answered with a clever condition: as many as can hold on to your cloak as you walk out. Tradition says he expected only a few.
So the Guru had a cloak made with fifty-two long tassels, one for each prince, and out through the gate they walked, all fifty-two, each holding a tassel.
For this, Sikhs call him Bandi Chhor, the one who frees the prisoners.
Tradition says he reached Amritsar around the time of Diwali, and the city lit lamps to welcome him.
That's why each autumn, while Hindus celebrate Diwali, Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, the day of release, and the Harmandir Sahib glows with lights and fireworks over the water.
One man's freedom, stretched wide enough for fifty-two.

how: Each autumn Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, remembering Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior with the fifty-two princes; gurdwaras, especially the Harmandir Sahib, are lit with lamps and lights.

practice: Sit still, and think of someone who is stuck right now: in a job, a debt, a sickness, a loneliness, a bad week.
Picture them clearly, and look for one tassel you could hand them, not the whole rescue, just a message, a ride, an introduction, an hour of your time. Choose it, and sit with the choice.

wordCard.voice: Bandi Chhor. The one who frees the prisoners, the title Sikhs gave Guru Hargobind after he walked fifty-two princes out of Gwalior fort on his cloak.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the liberator of prisoners, the title Sikhs give Guru Hargobind.

carryVoice: Your line: no one freed alone. Fifty-two tassels, one cloak, and nobody left behind. Sixty-seven days, and counting.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on Guru Hargobind's imprisonment at Gwalior and the release of the fifty-two rajas
